system: You are an expert reviewer of machine-learning research ideas.
user:
Compare two research ideas for the SAME research problem and pick the stronger one.

Research problem: Can MVFA's few-shot fusion be made inductive — scoring each image on its own, without the test-set min-max normalisation of the released code — without losing AUROC, and does this give a threshold that transfers to unseen modalities? The inductive fusion standardises each branch with leave-one-out statistics of the K normal support images (each support's zero-shot map, and its few-shot map against a memory bank built from the other K-1 supports, pooled over patches and levels), adds the standardised branches, and pools the fused map with the mean of its top 2% pixels; the threshold is the 95th percentile of the supports' leave-one-out image scores. Primary outcome: image- and pixel-level AUROC of inductive versus transductive fusion on every held-out modality and K in {2, 4, 8, 16}. Motivating measurement: the spread of the transductive AUROC across random test subsets and at 10% and 50% prevalence. Secondary outcomes: sensitivity, realised specificity, F1 and expected calibration error at the support-derived threshold. We also record whether the few-shot baselines compared in the target paper (APRIL-GAN, WinCLIP) normalise over the test set in their public code, to judge how widely the finding applies.

A stronger idea is one whose proposed change acts on the SPECIFIC mechanism of the target method that causes the problem (here: the released MVFA code and its verified behaviour), rather than a generic improvement that would apply to any anomaly detector.

Judge on:
1. Specificity. Would this idea plausibly solve THIS problem in THIS method better than a generic alternative? A mechanism that applies equally to any model and any problem is WEAKER, not stronger, because it does not explain why it fixes this problem.
2. Evidence. Is the proposed mechanism supported by the cited literature or by verified properties of the code and the benchmark?
3. Testability. Does the idea make a concrete, falsifiable prediction that can be checked on BMAD with one Colab GPU?

Explicitly DO NOT reward: length or polish of the write-up, stacking many modules, vague "add an attention/adapter module" proposals, or ideas that need data, labels or compute that are not available.

Idea A:
TITLE: Nearest-source-modality calibration transfer: calibrating an unseen modality with the source modalities its supports resemble
SUMMARY: Measure how similar the target's support normals are to each source modality in adapted feature space, and transfer the score-to-probability calibration learned on source episodes with weights proportional to that similarity.
HYPOTHESIS: Similarity-weighted transfer of source-episode calibrations reduces ECE on the held-out modality by at least 20% relative to a uniformly pooled source calibrator, and the improvement is largest for held-out modalities with a close source neighbour (e.g. LiverCT with BrainMRI as nearest source) and smallest for isolated ones (HIS).
RATIONALE: Both parents rely on a reference to decide what a score means — Fisher on the target's supports (normal side only), the episode calibrator on all source modalities equally (both sides). The reviewers questioned whether calibration learned on very different modalities transfers. A different explanation of transfer is similarity: calibration should transfer from source modalities whose normal feature distribution resembles the target's, which can be measured from the support normals alone. This gives a label-free, interpretable rule for how much each source modality should inform the target's calibration.
METHOD: 1) Per source modality m, fit a calibrator c_m (logistic on Fisher features) from source episodes as in the episode calibrator. 2) Similarity: mean adapted CLS feature of the target supports vs. each source modality's mean normal CLS feature; weights w_m = softmax(-d_m / T), d_m the cosine distance, T selected on source leave-one-source-out episodes. 3) Target probability p = sum_m w_m c_m(x). 4) Code: train_calibrator.py per modality; scoring.py similarity_weights().
EXPERIMENT: BMAD leave-one-modality-out (RESC and OCT17 held out together); MVFA checkpoints selected on source-modality validation splits and the MVFA baseline re-run the same way; K in {2,4,8,16}; 3 seeds x 3 support draws, mean and std. Baselines: pooled source calibrator; unweighted Fisher with support threshold; nearest-single-modality calibrator. Metrics: ECE, Brier, AUROC, similarity weights per fold, correlation between nearest-source distance and ECE. Falsification: no ECE gain over pooled calibration.

Idea B:
TITLE: Intra-image robust normalisation: each image as its own normal reference for per-image MVFA scoring
SUMMARY: Normalise every patch score of an image by the robust statistics (median and MAD) of that same image's patch scores, exploiting that most patches of any image are normal, and combine with a support-derived threshold.
HYPOTHESIS: Intra-image median/MAD normalisation of each branch's patch scores, fused per image, gives image AUROC within 1 point of MVFA's transductive fusion and reduces AUROC sensitivity to support draws (std across draws) by at least 30% compared with support-only LOO-Z at K = 2 and K = 4.
RATIONALE: The parent calibrates against the support normals, whose statistics are noisy at small K. By analogy with intrinsic-normal-prototype methods (an anomalous image still contains mostly normal tissue), each image provides its own large normal reference: its 289 patches per level. Robust statistics (median, MAD) are insensitive to the minority of anomalous patches, so standardising by them yields a per-image score that needs no test-set statistics and depends little on which supports were drawn. The supports are then used only for the operating threshold.
METHOD: 1) For each test image, branch b and level l: z_blj = (s_blj - median_j s_blj)/(1.4826 MAD_j s_blj + 1e-3). 2) Fused map F = sum over b, l of clip(z, -3, 10); image score = top-2% mean. 3) Threshold: 95th percentile of the same statistic on the support normals (LOO for the few-shot branch). 4) Diffuse anomalies covering more than 50% of an image violate the assumption: add the support-standardised global mean score as a second feature (max of the two after standardisation) as a safeguard. 5) Code: scoring.py intra_image_norm(); test_few.py; no retraining.
EXPERIMENT: BMAD leave-one-modality-out (RESC and OCT17 held out together); MVFA checkpoints selected on source-modality validation splits and the MVFA baseline re-run the same way; K in {2,4,8,16}; 3 seeds x 3 support draws, mean and std. Baselines: transductive MVFA; LOO-Z; augmentation-conformal calibration. Ablations: with/without the global safeguard; MAD vs IQR. Metrics: image/pixel AUROC, std of AUROC across support draws, realised FPR at the support threshold, performance on images with large lesions (mask area > 30%). Falsification: AUROC loss > 2 points or no reduction in draw sensitivity.

Respond in exactly this format:
REASONING: <one to three sentences explaining your choice>
CONFIDENCE: <HIGH | MEDIUM | LOW>
WINNER=<A | B | TIE>
